::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## How this checkpoint works
Part A is a quiz covering all of Module 2. In Part B you'll do a complete, realistic analysis: from the raw force signal of three jumps to the numbers a coach would receive. Links point back to the lessons if you need a refresher.

⏱️ About 40 minutes.
:::

## Part A · Quick quiz

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q1"}
A study reports *"Mean age 24.3 ± 3.1 years (mean ± SD) of the 18 participants"*. This is…

- [x] descriptive statistics
- [ ] inferential statistics

::: {.explanation}
It summarises the sample without generalising to a population. See [lesson 2.1](m2-01-what-is-statistics.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q2"}
**Training load measured as session-RPE (RPE × duration in minutes)**, e.g. 420 AU, is best treated as…

- [x] numerical (continuous)
- [ ] nominal
- [ ] ordinal

::: {.explanation}
Although RPE itself is a rating, session-RPE is a product with many possible values and is analysed as a numerical variable in practice.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q3"}
Ground contact times of a sprinter (ms): `98, 101, 97, 99, 180`. The 180 ms value came from a stumble. Which summary describes the *typical* contact time best?

- [ ] Mean
- [x] Median
- [ ] Range

::: {.explanation}
The median (99 ms) ignores the extreme value; the mean (115 ms) is pulled up by the stumble. See [lesson 2.2](m2-02-center.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q4"}
Squad A has a mean CMJ of 40 cm (SD 2 cm), squad B 40 cm (SD 6 cm). Which statement is correct?

- [ ] Squad B jumps higher
- [x] Jump heights vary much more between players in squad B
- [ ] Squad A has more outliers

::: {.explanation}
Same center, different spread. See [lesson 2.3](m2-03-spread.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q5"}
For a variable, Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 18. Is a value of 26 an outlier according to the IQR rule?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

::: {.explanation}
IQR = 18 − 12 = 6, so the upper fence is 18 + 1.5 × 6 = 27. A value of 26 is below the fence, so it is not flagged (although it is close). See [lesson 2.3](m2-03-spread.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.quiz id="cp2-q6"}
According to the central limit theorem, the standard error of a mean based on 9 trials is…

- [ ] the SD of single trials divided by 9
- [x] the SD of single trials divided by 3
- [ ] the same as the SD of single trials

::: {.explanation}
SE = SD / √n = SD / √9 = SD / 3. See [lesson 2.4](m2-04-normal-clt.qmd).
:::
:::

## Part B · From raw force to jump height

Athlete K's three CMJs are loaded in `cmj` (columns `trial`, `time_s`, `force_left`, `force_right`, `force_total`; 500 samples per second). Here are all three:

```{webr}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(cmj, aes(x = time_s, y = force_total)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ trial, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Vertical force (N)")
```

(`facet_wrap(~ trial)` draws one panel per trial. You'll learn more about facets in Module 3.)

### Step 1 · Body weight and data quality

Before analysing a jump you need the athlete's body weight, from a stable quiet-standing phase. Look at the plot: CMJ 1 and CMJ 3 start with a long, flat phase, but **CMJ 2** starts while the athlete is still settling on the plate.

::: {.task}
1. Create `quiet1`: rows of `cmj` for **CMJ 1** with `time_s <= 2`.
2. Create `quiet2`: rows of `cmj` for **CMJ 2** with `time_s <= 1` (its only "quiet" part).
3. Calculate the **SD** of `force_total` for each, and store them in `sd1` and `sd2`.
4. On the last line, calculate how many times larger `sd2` is than `sd1`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_1
#| caption: "Mini-project · Step 1"
# 1 and 2. Quiet-standing phases
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & ______)
quiet2 <- subset(cmj, ______ & ______)

# 3. SD of the force during quiet standing
sd1 <- ______
sd2 <- ______

# 4. How many times noisier is CMJ 2?
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="cp2_1"}
Combine conditions with `&`: `subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2" & time_s <= 1)`. Then `sd(quiet1$force_total)` and `sd2 / sd1`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="cp2_1"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_1
#| solution: true
# 1 and 2. Quiet-standing phases
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & time_s <= 2)
quiet2 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2" & time_s <= 1)

# 3. SD of the force during quiet standing
sd1 <- sd(quiet1$force_total)
sd2 <- sd(quiet2$force_total)

# 4. How many times noisier is CMJ 2?
sd2 / sd1
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_1
#| check: true
res <- .check_vars(c("quiet1", "quiet2", "sd1", "sd2"), .envir_result, .checker_args$envir_solution)
if (isTRUE(res$correct)) res <- .check_result(.result, .checker_args$solution,
  ok = paste0("Correct! The 'quiet' phase of CMJ 2 is about ", round(.checker_args$solution),
              " times more variable than that of CMJ 1. Its body weight estimate would be unreliable, so a good analyst uses the body weight from a clean trial (CMJ 1 or 3) instead."),
  no = "The SDs are right. The last line should be `sd2 / sd1`.")
res
```

### Step 2 · Flight time and jump height

During flight the force is (almost) zero. The **flight time** is the number of samples below a small threshold (we'll use **20 N**) multiplied by the time between samples (**0.002 s**). From the flight time *t*, physics gives the jump height:

$$h = \frac{g \, t^2}{8}, \qquad g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$$

::: {.task}
For **CMJ 1**:

1. Create `cmj1`, the rows of `cmj` for CMJ 1.
2. Calculate `flight_time` (s): the number of samples with `force_total < 20`, times 0.002. Tip: `sum()` of a logical vector counts the `TRUE`s.
3. Calculate `height_cm`, the jump height in **cm** (the formula gives metres, so multiply by 100).
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_2
#| caption: "Mini-project · Step 2"
# 1. Data of CMJ 1
cmj1 <- subset(cmj, ______)

# 2. Flight time (s)
flight_time <- sum(______) * 0.002

# 3. Jump height (cm)
height_cm <- ______

flight_time
height_cm
```

::: {.hint exercise="cp2_2"}
2. `sum(cmj1$force_total < 20) * 0.002`
3. `9.81 * flight_time^2 / 8 * 100`
:::

::: {.solution exercise="cp2_2"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_2
#| solution: true
# 1. Data of CMJ 1
cmj1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1")

# 2. Flight time (s)
flight_time <- sum(cmj1$force_total < 20) * 0.002

# 3. Jump height (cm)
height_cm <- 9.81 * flight_time^2 / 8 * 100

flight_time
height_cm
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_2
#| check: true
.check_vars(c("flight_time", "height_cm"), .envir_result, .checker_args$envir_solution,
  ok = "Correct! A flight time of 0.574 s gives a jump height of 40.4 cm, a strong jump for a basketball player.")
```

### Step 3 · Summarise the three jumps

Now do it for all three trials at once. `tapply()` (from [lesson 2.2](m2-02-center.qmd)) applies a function per trial.

::: {.task}
1. `flight` is calculated for you for each trial. Calculate the jump `heights` (cm) for all three trials, using the vector `flight`.
2. Calculate the mean (`mean_h`), standard deviation (`sd_h`) and coefficient of variation in % (`cv_h`) of the three heights.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_3
#| caption: "Mini-project · Step 3"
# Flight time per trial (s)
flight <- tapply(cmj$force_total < 20, cmj$trial, sum) * 0.002
flight

# 1. Jump heights (cm)
heights <- ______

# 2. Mean, SD and CV
mean_h <- ______
sd_h <- ______
cv_h <- ______

round(heights, 1)
c(mean = mean_h, sd = sd_h, cv = cv_h)
```

::: {.hint exercise="cp2_3"}
1. Arithmetic works on whole vectors: `9.81 * flight^2 / 8 * 100`
2. `mean(heights)`, `sd(heights)`, `sd_h / mean_h * 100`
:::

::: {.solution exercise="cp2_3"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_3
#| solution: true
# Flight time per trial (s)
flight <- tapply(cmj$force_total < 20, cmj$trial, sum) * 0.002
flight

# 1. Jump heights (cm)
heights <- 9.81 * flight^2 / 8 * 100

# 2. Mean, SD and CV
mean_h <- mean(heights)
sd_h <- sd(heights)
cv_h <- sd_h / mean_h * 100

round(heights, 1)
c(mean = mean_h, sd = sd_h, cv = cv_h)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_3
#| check: true
.check_vars(c("heights", "mean_h", "sd_h", "cv_h"), .envir_result, .checker_args$envir_solution,
  ok = "Excellent! Athlete K: 40.4 ± 0.9 cm (mean ± SD), CV ≈ 2.1 %. That's the kind of summary a coach receives after a testing session.")
```

### Step 4 · Left vs. right

A dual force platform also lets you compare the legs. During quiet standing, a healthy athlete usually carries roughly half their weight on each leg.

::: {.task}
Using `quiet1` (quiet standing in CMJ 1, given), calculate the **median** force under the left and the right foot (`left_med`, `right_med`). Then calculate the **percentage of body weight on the left leg**: `left_med / (left_med + right_med) * 100`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_4
#| caption: "Mini-project · Step 4"
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & time_s <= 2)

left_med <- ______
right_med <- ______

# Percentage of weight on the left leg
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="cp2_4"}
`median(quiet1$force_left)`, `median(quiet1$force_right)`, then `left_med / (left_med + right_med) * 100`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="cp2_4"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_4
#| solution: true
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & time_s <= 2)

left_med <- median(quiet1$force_left)
right_med <- median(quiet1$force_right)

# Percentage of weight on the left leg
left_med / (left_med + right_med) * 100
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: cp2_4
#| check: true
res <- .check_vars(c("left_med", "right_med"), .envir_result, .checker_args$envir_solution)
if (isTRUE(res$correct)) res <- .check_result(.result, .checker_args$solution,
  ok = paste0("Correct! In CMJ 1, Athlete K stood with about ", round(.checker_args$solution),
              " % of his weight on the left leg. Check CMJ 3 in the scratchpad: is it a consistent habit or just how he stood that time?"),
  no = "The medians are right. The last line should calculate the percentage on the left leg.")
res
```
